clinicalPearls: Second most common liposarcoma subtype, arising typically in the deep soft tissues of the thigh or popliteal fossa in young and middle-aged adults.
Defined by a recurrent FUS-DDIT3 fusion from t(12;16), with a small subset showing EWSR1-DDIT3; demonstrating this fusion confirms the diagnosis.
A higher proportion of hypercellular round-cell morphology denotes higher grade and worse prognosis; the round-cell component is the aggressive part of the spectrum.
Distinctively metastasises to unusual extrapulmonary soft-tissue and bone sites (spine, other soft tissues, retroperitoneum) as well as to the lungs.
Because of the propensity for spinal and soft-tissue metastases, whole-body MRI or dedicated axial imaging is often used for staging and surveillance.
Classic histology shows uniform round to oval cells in a myxoid stroma with a delicate plexiform (chicken-wire) capillary network and signet-ring lipoblasts.
Notably radiosensitive; neoadjuvant radiotherapy can produce marked tumour response and is frequently combined with wide surgical excision.
Sensitive to certain systemic agents such as trabectedin, which targets the fusion-driven transcriptional programme.
reference.pathophysiology: Myxoid liposarcoma is driven by a balanced translocation, most often t(12;16)(q13;p11), that fuses FUS with DDIT3 (CHOP); a minority carry an EWSR1-DDIT3 fusion. The chimeric protein acts as an aberrant transcription factor that dysregulates adipocytic differentiation by interfering with CCAAT/enhancer-binding proteins, arresting cells at an immature preadipocyte stage and promoting proliferation. The fusion also perturbs downstream pathways and cooperates with secondary events, notably activating alterations in the PI3K/AKT pathway (such as PIK3CA mutations and PTEN loss) and TERT promoter changes, which correlate with the transition to the hypercellular round-cell phenotype and more aggressive behaviour. The tumour's rich, delicate plexiform capillary vasculature and abundant myxoid matrix are characteristic and underlie its imaging appearance, sometimes mimicking a cyst. The distinctive tropism for extrapulmonary soft-tissue and bony metastatic sites reflects biology particular to this fusion-driven sarcoma rather than the lung-dominant spread of most sarcomas.
additionalDifferentials: Myxoid change within other soft-tissue sarcomas
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the primary site to assess fat content, myxoid matrix and local extent
Core needle biopsy with dedicated soft-tissue pathology review
FISH or RT-PCR for DDIT3 rearrangement (FUS-DDIT3 / EWSR1-DDIT3)
Histological quantification of the round-cell component for grading
Whole-body MRI or dedicated spinal imaging given extrapulmonary metastatic tropism
CT of the chest for pulmonary metastases
Assessment for suitability of neoadjuvant radiotherapy at a sarcoma centre
redFlags: A large or rapidly growing deep thigh mass in a young or middle-aged adult
New back pain or neurological symptoms suggesting spinal metastasis
Increasing round-cell content on repeat pathology indicating higher grade
Development of metastases at unusual soft-tissue or bony sites
Local recurrence after resection during surveillance
reference.prognosis: Pure or predominantly myxoid, low-grade tumours have a relatively favourable outcome, whereas a substantial round-cell (hypercellular) component markedly worsens prognosis and metastatic risk. Overall survival depends on grade, tumour size and metastatic status, and late relapses at extrapulmonary sites can occur.
pitfalls: Mistaking the myxoid, low-density imaging appearance for a benign cyst or myxoma and delaying biopsy.
Failing to quantify the round-cell component, which is essential for grading and prognosis.
Staging with chest CT alone and missing the characteristic spinal and soft-tissue metastases.
Overlooking the tumour's radiosensitivity, which influences the sequencing of neoadjuvant therapy.
Confusing it with other myxoid soft-tissue tumours without molecular confirmation of the DDIT3 fusion.
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Standard surgical and radiation oncology references for sarcoma
management: Perform wide surgical excision of the primary tumour with clear margins as the mainstay of curative treatment
Deliver neoadjuvant or adjuvant radiotherapy, exploiting the marked radiosensitivity of this subtype to improve local control and enable downsizing
Consider systemic therapy with anthracycline-based chemotherapy or trabectedin for round-cell-rich, large or metastatic disease
Grade by quantifying the round-cell component, which drives systemic treatment decisions and prognosis
Stage and survey with whole-body or dedicated spinal MRI plus chest CT, given the tropism for extrapulmonary soft-tissue, bone and spinal metastases
Manage through a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team with dedicated soft-tissue pathology confirming the FUS-DDIT3 fusion
Maintain prolonged surveillance for late and extrapulmonary relapse, with metastasectomy or targeted radiotherapy for oligometastatic disease
